newsitem.title: HAITI: Anti-government violence threatens Haitian economy.
newsitem.headline: Anti-government violence threatens Haitian economy.

text.p: International financial backers of Haiti's plans to privatise key industries, on a visit to assess the economy, said recent unrest and threats by groups opposed to privatisation could scare off investors.

After a week of anti-government demonstrations and a general strike that was violently enforced in some places, popular organisations announced last week that they would take to the streets again if their demands were not met.
"We will bring everything in this country to a stop," said a member of the Autonomous Centre of Haitian Workers at a news conference last week.

Earlier this month, dozens of popular organisations showed that they could shut the country down when they called a general strike. Despite government assurances that people would be protected on their way to work, most stayed home.

The protesters set up burning tire barricades, and used rocks and gunshots to enforce the strike. A carload of journalists narrowly escaped an angry mob in Cite Soleil, a Port-au-Prince slum. At an earlier protest, a man's hand was blown off by a police tear gas cannister.
"This is what a potential investor will read in a newspaper in the United States, creating a perception of instability," a World Bank official said.
"Discord here has taken the form of threats and barricades, as opposed to peaceful demonstrations," the official added. "That makes investors nervous."
The delegation, on a two-week visit, includes representatives of donor nations and international financial institutions.

The popular organisations have demanded the removal of Prime Minister Rosny Smarth, who they say is incompetent and incapable of relieving the misery in the impoverished country. Haiti has unemployment as high as 80 percent and the lowest wages in the hemisphere.
An official of Haiti's national bank agreed the unrest could hurt. "It brings widespread scepticism that the government can keep the peace and quiet," he said.
But both the Haitian bank official and the World Bank official said the government should go ahead with plans to privatise key state-run enterprises, which the popular organisations oppose.
"The government has no doubt it is pursuing the right policies," the World Bank official said.

The privatisation plan, already approved by parliament, provides for joint ventures, management contracts and concessions for the telephone and electric companies, the cement factory, the flour mill, the ports and the airport, among others.
The government hopes to attract private investment in addition to the hundreds of millions of dollars in international loans and grants that are conditioned on moves to privatise.

President Rene Preval has promised that the capital will be invested in infrastructure improvements that will turn the nation into a giant construction zone. But the anti-privatisation organisations have called the plan a sellout and accused the government of putting the demands of international donors above the needs of its own people.

Former President Jean-Bertrand Aristide, who was expected to run for office again in 2000, has also spoken out against privatisation. Some have taken his silence on the strikes to mean support for the popular groups.

Economists put some of the blame on the Aristide administration for Haiti's current financial woes. "The last administration left a mess on the financial side," economist Kesner Pharel said, citing a budget deficit of 1.2 billion gourdes ($86 million).
World Bank officials say the Preval/Smarth government has been disciplined in its spending and has created a budget surplus.

Until parliament approves this year's budget, public spending is limited to the amounts dictated by the 1996 budget under which only $25 million can be spent monthly on wages and operations. The proposed 1997 budget would allocate $30 million monthly.
